quizzes.title: Checkpoint 1 — APIs, HTTP Methods, and Resources
quizzes.intro: Check whether you understand API contracts, method intent, and resource URL thinking.

questions.prompt: In beginner terms, what is an API?

options.text: A contract that lets one program communicate with another in defined ways
A type of monitor cable
A CSS animation preset
A physical server rack label only

questions.explanation: APIs define how software talks—requests, responses, and rules—especially over HTTP on the web.

wrongExplanations.b: Cables are hardware, not application interfaces.
wrongExplanations.c: CSS animations are unrelated to API contracts.
wrongExplanations.d: While APIs may run on servers, the API itself is the interface contract.

questions.prompt: Which HTTP method is primarily used to read a resource without changing server state?

options.text: DELETE
GET
PATCH
PUT

questions.explanation: GET is the standard safe read method for resources and collections.

questions.prompt: Which URL style best matches resource-oriented REST thinking for a lesson collection?

options.text: /api/createLessonNowPlease
/api/lessons
/api/doSomethingRandom
/api/runJavaScriptOnServer

questions.explanation: Collections are typically plural nouns; methods carry the verb.

wrongExplanations.a: Verb-heavy paths often lean RPC-style and duplicate what POST already means.
wrongExplanations.c: Vague action paths hide the resource model.
wrongExplanations.d: That describes an implementation urge, not a resource name.

questions.prompt: What does it mean that a well-designed GET is safe/idempotent in practical beginner terms?

options.text: Repeating the GET should not change server state as a side effect of reading
GET always deletes duplicates automatically
GET cannot return JSON
GET requires a request body every time

questions.explanation: Reads should not mutate resources; that expectation powers caching and retries.

questions.prompt: In a typical HTTP API exchange, what does the server return after processing a request?

options.text: An HTTP response with a status code and often headers and a body
Only a CSS file forever
A silent void with no status information by definition
A Git commit hash exclusively

questions.explanation: Responses communicate outcome via status codes plus optional headers and bodies.

wrongExplanations.b: APIs may return many content types; not only CSS.
wrongExplanations.d: Commit hashes are version-control concepts, not the general response definition.

quizzes.title: Checkpoint 2 — Status Codes, JSON, and Auth Basics
quizzes.intro: Test status interpretation, JSON payloads, parameters, and authentication/authorization basics.

questions.prompt: Which status code most clearly indicates a resource could not be found?
questions.explanation: 404 Not Found signals the targeted resource is missing.

wrongExplanations.d: 301 is a redirect, not a missing-resource error.

options.text: They are exact synonyms in every API
401 usually means authentication is missing/invalid; 403 means the caller is not allowed to perform the action
403 means success and 401 means created
401 means the JSON was pretty-printed

questions.explanation: 401 is about identity/credentials; 403 is about permission after identity is known (in common usage).

wrongExplanations.a: They communicate different problems in standard practice.
wrongExplanations.d: Pretty-printing is unrelated to status codes.

questions.prompt: Why should secret API keys not be embedded in public frontend code?

options.text: Because browsers can be inspected and secrets would be exposed
Because JSON cannot travel over HTTPS
Because frontend code cannot make HTTP requests
Because status codes stop working when keys exist

questions.explanation: Anything shipped to the browser can be viewed; keep privileged secrets on the server.

wrongExplanations.b: JSON over HTTPS is common and valid.
wrongExplanations.d: Keys do not disable status codes.

questions.prompt: What are query parameters commonly used for on collection endpoints?

options.text: Filtering, sorting, and pagination of results
Replacing HTTPS with FTP automatically
Deleting the server access logs by default
Compiling TypeScript on the client

questions.explanation: Query strings refine collection reads without inventing a new resource path for every variation.

wrongExplanations.b: Query params do not switch protocols that way.
wrongExplanations.c: They are not a log-deletion mechanism.
wrongExplanations.d: Compilation is unrelated to query-string filtering.

questions.prompt: Why are consistent machine-readable error envelopes valuable?

options.text: They let every client invent a different parsing strategy for fun
They help clients handle failures uniformly instead of scraping random message strings
They remove the need for status codes entirely
They guarantee zero bugs in business logic

questions.explanation: A stable error shape with codes/fields makes robust client handling possible.

wrongExplanations.a: Consistency reduces inventiveness tax, not increases it.
wrongExplanations.d: Error formats improve communication; they do not eliminate logic bugs.

quizzes.title: Final Quiz — Evolution, Retries, and Judgment
quizzes.intro: Apply API judgment to pagination, retries, debugging, and real-world design tradeoffs.

questions.prompt: Why do list endpoints usually need pagination?

options.text: Because JSON cannot represent arrays
Because datasets grow and returning everything in one response becomes slow and fragile
Because HTTP forbids arrays without page numbers
Because status codes only work on page 1

questions.explanation: Pagination keeps responses bounded as data scales.

wrongExplanations.c: HTTP does not require page numbers by law of the protocol.
wrongExplanations.d: Status codes work regardless of page index.

questions.prompt: Why can retrying a POST create problem without safeguards?

options.text: Because POST can create a new resource on each attempt, risking duplicates
Because POST can never send JSON
Because servers ignore POST after the first millisecond always
Because POST deletes pagination metadata automatically

questions.explanation: Non-idempotent creates may duplicate on network retries unless idempotency keys or constraints exist.

wrongExplanations.c: Servers process POST normally; the issue is duplicate side effects.
wrongExplanations.d: POST does not inherently delete pagination metadata.

questions.prompt: curl succeeds but the browser frontend fails calling the same API. What is a common culprit?

options.text: CORS restrictions in the browser that curl does not enforce the same way
JSON being illegal in browsers
HTTP methods not existing in browsers
Status code 200 being impossible in browsers

questions.explanation: Browsers enforce cross-origin rules; tooling outside the browser may not show the same failure.

wrongExplanations.c: Browsers support HTTP methods via XHR/fetch.

questions.prompt: What is a safer approach when evolving a public API used by external clients?

options.text: Rename and remove fields freely with no notice
Prefer additive changes, document deprecations, and version breaking changes carefully
Change status code meanings weekly for creativity
Put admin secrets in example snippets on the public docs homepage

questions.explanation: Compatibility and communication prevent breaking dependent clients.

wrongExplanations.d: Publishing secrets is a security failure.

questions.prompt: When debugging a failed call, what should you inspect first among these options?

options.text: The HTTP status code and whether the request URL/method/headers match the docs
Only the favicon of the marketing site
The laptop’s wallpaper color
Whether the JSON keys are alphabetized for beauty

questions.explanation: Status plus request shape quickly separates client mistakes from server failures.

wrongExplanations.b: Favicons do not explain API failures.
wrongExplanations.d: Key order in JSON objects is not the primary correctness signal.

questions.prompt: A response returns HTTP 200 with a body `{ "ok": false, "error": "invalid price" }`. What does that teach?

options.text: Network transport succeeded, but you must still handle business-level failure in the body
HTTP 200 always means the business operation succeeded
The client should ignore the body forever
Status codes are meaningless in REST

questions.explanation: Some APIs embed success flags in bodies; clients must interpret both status and payload—though clearer status usage is often better design.

wrongExplanations.b: This example shows 200 can still carry a failed business result.
wrongExplanations.c: The body contains the failure detail.
wrongExplanations.d: Status codes remain meaningful even when bodies add detail.
